Prof Q/ ELEC 10314 problems
We’ll work through these together in class.
Problem 1
Ch. 1 — Scientific and Engineering Notation
A capacitor has a value of $0.000\,000\,1\ \text{F}$. Express this value in scientific notation and in engineering notation (exponent a multiple of 3). Then write it using the matching metric prefix.
Write $0.000\,000\,1\ \text{F}$ in scientific notation, in engineering notation, and with a metric prefix.
$1 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{F} = 100 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{F} = 100\ \text{nF}$ F
Step 1Given $C = 0.000\,000\,1\ \text{F}$.
Step 2Scientific notation: move the decimal point 7 places right: $C = 1 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{F}$.
Step 3Engineering notation: the nearest multiple of 3 below $-7$ is $-9$, so $C = 100 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{F}$.
Step 4The prefix for $10^{-9}$ is nano: $$C = 100\ \text{nF}$$
Worked Solution
Given: $C = 0.000\,000\,1\ \text{F}$. Scientific notation: move the decimal point 7 places right to reach the digit 1, so $C = 1 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{F}$. Engineering notation: $-7$ is not a multiple of 3. Moving the decimal 2 more places right gives 100 with exponent $-9$: $C = 100 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{F}$. The prefix for $10^{-9}$ is nano (n): $$C = 1 \times 10^{-7}\ \text{F} = 100 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{F} = 100\ \text{nF}$$
Problem 2
Ch. 1 — Metric-Prefix Conversion
A datasheet lists a pull-up resistor as $2.2 \times 10^{5}\ \Omega$. Your parts list uses megohms. Convert the value to megohms, showing the powers of ten involved, and also write it in kilohms as a check.
Convert $2.2 \times 10^{5}\ \Omega$ to $\text{M}\Omega$ (and check in $\text{k}\Omega$).
0.22 MΩ
Step 1Given $R = 2.2 \times 10^{5}\ \Omega$, with mega $= 10^{6}$ and kilo $= 10^{3}$.
Step 2Divide by $10^{6}$ for megohms: $$R = \frac{2.2 \times 10^{5}}{10^{6}}\ \text{M}\Omega = 0.22\ \text{M}\Omega$$
Step 3Check: $2.2 \times 10^{5}/10^{3} = 220\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Step 4Since $1\ \text{M}\Omega = 1\,000\ \text{k}\Omega$, $220\ \text{k}\Omega = 0.22\ \text{M}\Omega$.
Worked Solution
Given: $R = 2.2 \times 10^{5}\ \Omega$. Mega means $10^{6}$, so divide by $10^{6}$: $$R = \frac{2.2 \times 10^{5}}{10^{6}}\ \text{M}\Omega = 2.2 \times 10^{-1}\ \text{M}\Omega = 0.22\ \text{M}\Omega$$ Check in kilohms, where kilo means $10^{3}$: $R = \frac{2.2 \times 10^{5}}{10^{3}}\ \text{k}\Omega = 220\ \text{k}\Omega$. Since $1\ \text{M}\Omega = 1\,000\ \text{k}\Omega$, $220\ \text{k}\Omega = 0.22\ \text{M}\Omega$, which is consistent.
Problem 3
Ch. 1 — Significant Figures in Multi-Step Calculations
Relative to ground, point A in a circuit is measured at $8.426\ \text{V}$ and point B at $2.1\ \text{V}$. A charge of $0.0350\ \text{C}$ moves from A to B. The energy transferred is $W = V_{AB}\, Q$, where $V_{AB} = V_A - V_B$. Find $W$ and report it with the correct number of significant figures. Carry unrounded intermediate values, and state which rule and which measurement limits each step.
Find $V_{AB}$, then the energy $W$ in joules, reported to the correct significant figures.
0.22 J
Step 1Given $V_A = 8.426\ \text{V}$, $V_B = 2.1\ \text{V}$, $Q = 0.0350\ \text{C}$.
Step 2Subtract: $V_{AB} = 8.426 - 2.1 = 6.326\ \text{V}$.
Step 3Subtraction rule: $2.1\ \text{V}$ limits the result to tenths, so $V_{AB} \approx 6.3\ \text{V}$ (2 sig figs). Keep 6.326 as a guard digit.
Step 4Multiply: $$W = (6.326\ \text{V})(0.0350\ \text{C}) = 0.221\,41\ \text{J}$$
Step 5Multiplication rule: 2 sig figs is the fewest, so $W = 0.22\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $V_A = 8.426\ \text{V}$, $V_B = 2.1\ \text{V}$, $Q = 0.0350\ \text{C}$. Step 1 (subtraction, where the least precise decimal place governs): $V_{AB} = 8.426 - 2.1 = 6.326\ \text{V}$. The value $2.1\ \text{V}$ is known only to the tenths place, so $V_{AB}$ is good to $6.3\ \text{V}$, which is 2 significant figures. Keep 6.326 as a guard value. Step 2 (multiplication, where the fewest significant figures govern): $$W = V_{AB}\, Q = (6.326\ \text{V})(0.0350\ \text{C}) = 0.221\,41\ \text{V}\cdot\text{C}$$ Units: $\text{V}\cdot\text{C} = (\text{J/C})\cdot\text{C} = \text{J}$. $V_{AB}$ has 2 significant figures and $Q$ has 3, so $W$ keeps 2: $$W = 0.22\ \text{J}$$ The subtraction reduced a 4-significant-figure reading to a 2-significant-figure difference.
Problem 4
Ch. 1 — Unit Conversion
A lab bench power supply used $1.5\ \text{kWh}$ of energy during a semester. Given $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$ and $1\ \text{h} = 3\,600\ \text{s}$, convert this energy to joules. Express the result in scientific notation and with a metric prefix.
Convert $1.5\ \text{kWh}$ to joules.
5.4e6 J
Step 1Given $W = 1.5\ \text{kWh}$, with $1\ \text{W} = 1\ \text{J/s}$ and $1\ \text{h} = 3\,600\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Remove the prefix: $1.5\ \text{kW} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J/s}$.
Step 3Multiply by the time in seconds: $$W = (1.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J/s})(3\,600\ \text{s}) = 5.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$$
Step 4With a prefix: $W = 5.4\ \text{MJ}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $W = 1.5\ \text{kWh}$. Remove the prefix: $1.5\ \text{kW} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{W} = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\ \text{J/s}$. Convert hours to seconds: $$W = 1.5 \times 10^{3}\ \frac{\text{J}}{\text{s}} \times 1\ \text{h} \times \frac{3\,600\ \text{s}}{1\ \text{h}} = 5.4 \times 10^{6}\ \text{J}$$ With a prefix: $W = 5.4\ \text{MJ}$.
Problem 5
Ch. 1 — Reported Precision and Uncertainty
A bench meter displays a current of $0.338\,16\ \text{mA}$. The accuracy specification for this range is $\pm 1\%$ of the reading. Compute the uncertainty and round it to one significant figure. Then report the current in the form value $\pm$ uncertainty, keeping only the digits the uncertainty justifies.
Report the current with appropriate precision in the form $I \pm \Delta I$.
0.338 ± 0.003 mA
Step 1Given $I = 0.338\,16\ \text{mA}$ with accuracy $\pm 1\%$ of reading.
Step 2Compute the uncertainty: $\Delta I = 0.01 \times 0.338\,16 = 0.003\,38\ \text{mA}$.
Step 3Round the uncertainty to one significant figure: $\Delta I \approx 0.003\ \text{mA}$, in the thousandths place.
Step 4Round the reading to the same place: $0.338\,16 \rightarrow 0.338\ \text{mA}$.
Step 5Report: $$I = 0.338 \pm 0.003\ \text{mA} = 338 \pm 3\ \mu\text{A}$$
Worked Solution
Given: reading $I = 0.338\,16\ \text{mA}$ and accuracy $\pm 1\%$ of reading. Uncertainty: $$\Delta I = 0.01 \times 0.338\,16\ \text{mA} = 0.003\,381\,6\ \text{mA}$$ Rounded to one significant figure: $\Delta I \approx 0.003\ \text{mA}$. The uncertainty is in the thousandths place, so round the reading to the thousandths: $0.338\,16 \rightarrow 0.338\ \text{mA}$. Reported result: $$I = 0.338 \pm 0.003\ \text{mA}$$ In microamperes, that is $338 \pm 3\ \mu\text{A}$.
Problem 6
Ch. 1 — Calculations in Powers of Ten
Without converting to ordinary decimals, evaluate $$X = \frac{(2.40 \times 10^{-6})(3.30 \times 10^{4})}{(8.00 \times 10^{-3})(1.50 \times 10^{2})}$$ Handle the coefficients and the powers of ten separately. Give the result in scientific notation and in engineering notation, and name the matching metric prefix. Report 3 significant figures.
Evaluate $X$ in scientific and engineering notation, and name the matching metric prefix.
$6.60 \times 10^{-2} = 66.0 \times 10^{-3}$ (milli)
Step 1Numerator: $(2.40)(3.30) = 7.92$ and $10^{-6+4} = 10^{-2}$, giving $7.92 \times 10^{-2}$.
Step 2Denominator: $(8.00)(1.50) = 12.0$ and $10^{-3+2} = 10^{-1}$, giving $12.0 \times 10^{-1} = 1.20 \times 10^{0}$.
Step 3Divide: $$X = \frac{7.92}{1.20} \times 10^{-2-0} = 6.60 \times 10^{-2}$$
Step 4Engineering form: $66.0 \times 10^{-3}$. The prefix is milli (m), so $X = 66.0\ \text{m}$ to 3 sig figs.
Worked Solution
Numerator: $(2.40)(3.30) = 7.92$ and $10^{-6} \times 10^{4} = 10^{-2}$, so the numerator is $7.92 \times 10^{-2}$. Denominator: $(8.00)(1.50) = 12.0$ and $10^{-3} \times 10^{2} = 10^{-1}$, so the denominator is $12.0 \times 10^{-1} = 1.20 \times 10^{0}$. Divide: $$X = \frac{7.92}{1.20} \times 10^{-2-0} = 6.60 \times 10^{-2}$$ Engineering notation: $6.60 \times 10^{-2} = 66.0 \times 10^{-3}$. The prefix for $10^{-3}$ is milli (m), so $X = 66.0\ \text{m}$. All inputs have 3 significant figures, so the result keeps 3.
Problem 7
Ch. 2 — Voltage as Energy per Charge
A battery does $36\ \text{J}$ of work to move $4.0\ \text{C}$ of charge from its negative terminal to its positive terminal. Using $V = W/Q$, find the battery's voltage, and state in words what that value means.
Find the voltage $V$ and interpret it.
9.0 V
Step 1Given $W = 36\ \text{J}$ and $Q = 4.0\ \text{C}$.
Step 2Use the definition of voltage: $V = W/Q$.
Step 3Substitute: $$V = \frac{36\ \text{J}}{4.0\ \text{C}} = 9.0\ \text{J/C} = 9.0\ \text{V}$$
Step 4Interpretation: each coulomb gains $9.0\ \text{J}$ of energy passing through the battery.
Worked Solution
Given: $W = 36\ \text{J}$ and $Q = 4.0\ \text{C}$. Voltage is energy per unit charge: $$V = \frac{W}{Q} = \frac{36\ \text{J}}{4.0\ \text{C}} = 9.0\ \text{J/C} = 9.0\ \text{V}$$ Interpretation: the battery gives 9.0 joules of energy to every coulomb of charge it moves through it.
Problem 8
Ch. 2 — 5-Band Resistor Color Code and Tolerance
A 5-band precision resistor has the bands orange, orange, black, red, brown, read from left to right. The color code is: black 0, brown 1, red 2, orange 3, yellow 4, green 5, blue 6, violet 7, gray 8, white 9. On a 5-band resistor, the first three bands are digits, the fourth is the multiplier, and the fifth is the tolerance, where brown means $\pm 1\%$. Decode the nominal value and tolerance, and find the acceptable range. Give the minimum in-tolerance resistance as your final answer, and state whether a part measuring $32.5\ \text{k}\Omega$ passes.
Decode the resistor, find its tolerance range, give the minimum in-tolerance resistance in kilohms, and judge a $32.5\ \text{k}\Omega$ reading.
32.67 kΩ
Step 1Digit bands: orange, orange, black $= 3, 3, 0$, giving 330.
Step 2Multiplier band, red, is $10^{2}$: $R = 330 \times 10^{2} = 33\,000\ \Omega = 33.0\ \text{k}\Omega$.
Step 3Tolerance band, brown, means $\pm 1\%$: $\Delta R = 0.01 \times 33\,000 = 330\ \Omega$.
Step 4Range: $$R_{\min} = 32.67\ \text{k}\Omega, \quad R_{\max} = 33.33\ \text{k}\Omega$$
Step 5Since $32.5\ \text{k}\Omega < 32.67\ \text{k}\Omega$, the part is out of tolerance.
Worked Solution
Digit bands: orange $= 3$, orange $= 3$, black $= 0$, giving 330. Multiplier band: red $= 10^{2}$. Nominal: $R = 330 \times 10^{2}\ \Omega = 33\,000\ \Omega = 33.0\ \text{k}\Omega$. Tolerance band: brown $= \pm 1\%$, so $\Delta R = 0.01 \times 33\,000 = 330\ \Omega$. Range: $$R_{\min} = 33\,000 - 330 = 32\,670\ \Omega = 32.67\ \text{k}\Omega$$ $$R_{\max} = 33\,000 + 330 = 33\,330\ \Omega = 33.33\ \text{k}\Omega$$ A reading of $32.5\ \text{k}\Omega$ is below $32.67\ \text{k}\Omega$, so the part is out of tolerance and fails.
Problem 9
Ch. 2 — DMM Current Range, Resolution, and Accuracy
A manual-ranging $3\tfrac{1}{2}$-digit DMM (maximum display 1999 counts) has DC current ranges of 2 mA, 20 mA, and 200 mA. The true current in a circuit is $0.8472\ \text{mA}$. Determine what the display shows on each range, and choose the range with the best resolution. On that range, the accuracy specification is $\pm(1.0\%\ \text{of reading} + 3\ \text{counts})$. Compute the worst-case uncertainty of the reading in milliamperes.
DMM DC current ranges (3½-digit, 1999 counts)
Range     Max display   Resolution (1 count)
2 mA      1.999 mA      0.001 mA
20 mA     19.99 mA      0.01 mA
200 mA    199.9 mA      0.1 mA
Find the display on each range, choose the best range, and compute the worst-case uncertainty on that range.
0.0115 mA
Step 12 mA range: $0.8472 < 1.999$, so no overload. The display shows $0.847\ \text{mA}$.
Step 220 mA range: the resolution is $0.01\ \text{mA}$, so the display shows $0.85\ \text{mA}$.
Step 3200 mA range: the resolution is $0.1\ \text{mA}$, so the display shows $0.8\ \text{mA}$.
Step 4Best range: 2 mA, which has the finest resolution without overload.
Step 5Uncertainty: $$\Delta I = 0.010(0.847) + 3(0.001) = 0.008\,47 + 0.003 = 0.011\,47\ \text{mA}$$
Step 6Result: $\Delta I \approx 0.0115\ \text{mA}$, so the reading is $0.847 \pm 0.011\ \text{mA}$.
Worked Solution
2 mA range: $0.8472 < 1.999$, so there is no overload. The resolution is $0.001\ \text{mA}$, so the display shows $0.847\ \text{mA}$. 20 mA range: the resolution is $0.01\ \text{mA}$, so the display shows $0.85\ \text{mA}$. 200 mA range: the resolution is $0.1\ \text{mA}$, so the display shows $0.8\ \text{mA}$. The best range is 2 mA, the lowest range that does not overload, which shows three significant digits. Uncertainty on the 2 mA range, where one count is $0.001\ \text{mA}$: $$\Delta I = 0.010 \times 0.847\ \text{mA} + 3 \times 0.001\ \text{mA} = 0.008\,47 + 0.003 = 0.011\,47\ \text{mA}$$ So $\Delta I \approx 0.0115\ \text{mA}$, or about $\pm 0.01\ \text{mA}$. The reading is $0.847 \pm 0.011\ \text{mA}$, and the true value lies between about 0.836 and $0.858\ \text{mA}$.
Problem 10
Ch. 2 — Setting Up a Voltage Measurement
A series circuit contains a battery B1, resistor R1, and resistor R2. Node A is at the positive terminal of B1, node B is between R1 and R2, and node C is between R2 and the negative terminal of B1. You must measure the voltage across R2 with a digital multimeter while the circuit is powered. Describe, in order, how you prepare the meter and where you place the probes. State how the reading's sign tells you the polarity.
Series circuit for measuring the voltage across R2
Describe the meter setup and probe placement for measuring the voltage across R2, and explain how to read the polarity.
(1) Set the DMM to DC volts on a range above the battery voltage, or use autorange. (2) Put the black lead in COM and the red lead in the V/Ω jack. Make sure the red lead is not in an A or mA jack. (3) Leave the circuit intact, since no wires are broken for a voltage measurement. (4) Place the probes in parallel with R2: red on node B and black on node C. (5) Read the display, stepping down the range for better resolution if needed. A positive reading means node B is positive with respect to node C. A negative sign means the probes are reversed relative to the actual polarity.
Step 1Voltage is measured in parallel across the component, and the circuit stays intact.
Step 2Set the DMM to DC volts on a range above the source voltage, or use autorange.
Step 3Put black in COM and red in V/Ω, never in a current jack.
Step 4Place red on node B and black on node C, across R2.
Step 5Read the display, adjusting the range if needed. The meter shows $V_{red} - V_{black}$, so a positive value means B is positive with respect to C, and a negative sign means the probes are reversed.
Worked Solution
A voltmeter measures the potential difference between two points, so it connects in parallel with the component and the circuit is not broken. Procedure: (1) Select DC voltage on a range greater than the battery voltage, or use autorange. (2) Insert black into COM and red into V/Ω. A lead left in a current jack would short R2. (3) With the circuit powered, touch the red probe to node B, the end of R2 nearer the positive side, and the black probe to node C. (4) Read the value, moving to a lower range if that improves resolution without overload. (5) Interpretation: the DMM displays $V_{red} - V_{black}$. A positive reading confirms node B is at a higher potential than node C, and a minus sign means the probes are reversed.
Problem 11
Ch. 2 — Shock-Current Safety Reasoning
While probing a $120\ \text{V}$ supply with damaged test leads, a technician with sweaty hands touches an exposed conductor with one hand and a grounded chassis with the other. Take the hand-to-hand body resistance under these conditions as $1\,200\ \Omega$. Using $I = V/R$, estimate the current through the body in milliamperes. Compare it with these approximate thresholds: about $1\ \text{mA}$ is perceptible, about $10\text{–}20\ \text{mA}$ causes loss of muscle control (cannot let go), and about $100\ \text{mA}$ can cause ventricular fibrillation. Explain which safety practices would have prevented the exposure.
Estimate the body current, compare it with the thresholds, and state the safety practices that prevent the hazard.
100 mA
Step 1Given $V = 120\ \text{V}$ and $R_{body} = 1\,200\ \Omega$.
Step 2Estimate the current: $$I = \frac{120}{1\,200} = 0.100\ \text{A} = 100\ \text{mA}$$
Step 3Compare: $100\ \text{mA}$ is far above the $10\text{–}20\ \text{mA}$ can't-let-go level and in the fibrillation range. A hand-to-hand path crosses the heart.
Step 4Moisture lowers body resistance and raises the current.
Step 5Prevention: inspect and replace damaged leads, use CAT-rated equipment, de-energize and verify, follow the one-hand rule, avoid grounded contact, and keep hands dry.
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 120\ \text{V}$ and $R_{body} = 1\,200\ \Omega$. Estimated current: $$I = \frac{V}{R} = \frac{120\ \text{V}}{1\,200\ \Omega} = 0.100\ \text{A} = 100\ \text{mA}$$ Comparison: this is about 100 times the perception threshold and well beyond the can't-let-go level. It reaches the range that can cause ventricular fibrillation. The hand-to-hand path also crosses the chest, which makes it especially dangerous. Moisture lowers skin resistance, which raises the current. Prevention: inspect the leads before use and replace damaged ones; use meters and leads with the proper CAT rating; de-energize and verify the circuit before touching conductors; keep one hand away from the circuit (the one-hand rule) and avoid contact with grounded metal; keep hands dry and remove jewelry.
Problem 12
Ch. 2 — Current, Charge, Electrons, and Energy
A $6.0\ \text{V}$ source supplies a steady current of $250\ \text{mA}$ to a lamp for $8.0\ \text{min}$. Use $I = Q/t$, $V = W/Q$, and the constant $1\ \text{C} \approx 6.25 \times 10^{18}$ electrons. Find the charge delivered, the number of electrons that passed through the lamp, and the energy the source supplied. Give the energy as your final answer.
Find $Q$, the number of electrons, and the energy $W$. The energy is the final answer.
720 J
Step 1Given $V = 6.0\ \text{V}$, $I = 0.250\ \text{A}$, $t = 8.0\ \text{min} = 480\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Charge: $$Q = I t = (0.250)(480) = 120\ \text{C}$$
Step 3Electrons: $n = 120 \times 6.25 \times 10^{18} = 7.5 \times 10^{20}$.
Step 4Energy: $$W = V Q = (6.0)(120) = 720\ \text{J}$$
Step 5Units check: $\text{A}\cdot\text{s} = \text{C}$ and $\text{V}\cdot\text{C} = \text{J}$. So $W = 7.2 \times 10^{2}\ \text{J}$.
Worked Solution
Given: $V = 6.0\ \text{V}$, $I = 250\ \text{mA} = 0.250\ \text{A}$, $t = 8.0\ \text{min} = 480\ \text{s}$. Charge, rearranging $I = Q/t$: $$Q = I t = (0.250\ \text{A})(480\ \text{s}) = 120\ \text{C}$$ Electrons: $n = 120 \times 6.25 \times 10^{18} = 7.5 \times 10^{20}$ electrons. Energy, rearranging $V = W/Q$: $$W = V Q = (6.0\ \text{J/C})(120\ \text{C}) = 720\ \text{J}$$ Units check: $\text{A}\cdot\text{s} = \text{C}$ and $(\text{J/C})\cdot\text{C} = \text{J}$. To 2 significant figures, $W = 7.2 \times 10^{2}\ \text{J}$.
Problem 13
Integrated — Current from Logged Charge Data
A charge-counting instrument logged the total (cumulative) charge that passed through a wire, as shown in the exhibit. Using $I = Q/t$, find the average current over the full $8.0\ \text{s}$ record in milliamperes. Then check whether the current was roughly constant by computing the current over the first and last $2.0\ \text{s}$ intervals. Convert units explicitly.
Cumulative charge log
Time (s)   Cumulative charge (mC)
0.0        0.0
2.0        15.2
4.0        30.1
6.0        45.3
8.0        60.4
Find the average current over $8.0\ \text{s}$, and check it against the first and last intervals.
7.6 mA
Step 1Total charge: $Q = 60.4\ \text{mC} = 60.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}$ over $t = 8.0\ \text{s}$.
Step 2Average current: $$I_{avg} = \frac{60.4 \times 10^{-3}}{8.0} = 7.55 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} \approx 7.6\ \text{mA}$$
Step 3First interval: $15.2\ \text{mC}/2.0\ \text{s} = 7.6\ \text{mA}$.
Step 4Last interval: $(60.4 - 45.3)/2.0 = 7.55\ \text{mA}$.
Step 5The intervals agree with the average, so the current was essentially constant at about $7.6\ \text{mA}$.
Worked Solution
Total charge: $Q = 60.4\ \text{mC} = 60.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}$, and $t = 8.0\ \text{s}$. Average current: $$I_{avg} = \frac{60.4 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{C}}{8.0\ \text{s}} = 7.55 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{A} = 7.55\ \text{mA} \approx 7.6\ \text{mA}$$ The result has 2 significant figures because $t = 8.0\ \text{s}$ does. First interval: $(15.2 - 0.0)\ \text{mC} / 2.0\ \text{s} = 7.6\ \text{mA}$. Last interval: $(60.4 - 45.3)\ \text{mC} / 2.0\ \text{s} = 15.1/2.0 = 7.55\ \text{mA}$. Both intervals match the average, so the current was essentially constant.
Problem 14
Integrated — Adding Quantities with Different Prefixes
Three sources are connected in series, aiding, so their voltages add. Their voltages are $V_1 = 0.0120\ \text{kV}$, $V_2 = 850\ \text{mV}$, and $V_3 = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\ \mu\text{V}$. Convert each to volts, find the total voltage, and report it with correct precision.
Convert each voltage to volts and find the total, reported with correct precision.
15.4 V
Step 1$V_1 = 0.0120\ \text{kV} = 0.0120 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V} = 12.0\ \text{V}$.
Step 2$V_2 = 850\ \text{mV} = 850 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} = 0.850\ \text{V}$.
Step 3$V_3 = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\ \mu\text{V} = 2.5 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-6}\ \text{V} = 2.5\ \text{V}$.
Step 4Add: $$V_T = 12.0 + 0.850 + 2.5 = 15.35\ \text{V}$$
Step 5The tenths place limits the sum: $V_T = 15.4\ \text{V}$.
Worked Solution
Convert each voltage to volts. $V_1 = 0.0120\ \text{kV} = 0.0120 \times 10^{3}\ \text{V} = 12.0\ \text{V}$. $V_2 = 850\ \text{mV} = 850 \times 10^{-3}\ \text{V} = 0.850\ \text{V}$. $V_3 = 2.5 \times 10^{6}\ \mu\text{V} = 2.5 \times 10^{6} \times 10^{-6}\ \text{V} = 2.5\ \text{V}$. Sum: $$V_T = 12.0 + 0.850 + 2.5 = 15.35\ \text{V}$$ Precision: $12.0\ \text{V}$ and $2.5\ \text{V}$ are known only to the tenths place, so round to tenths: $V_T = 15.4\ \text{V}$.
